main.title: inFAMOUS: Festival of Blood
main.subtitle: Zeke tells a story with a darker bite
main.summary: inFAMOUS: Festival of Blood is Sucker Punch's standalone PlayStation 3 action game, first released in North America on 25 October 2011. Zeke recounts an exaggerated tale in which Cole MacGrath becomes a vampire, turning the familiar city and powers of inFAMOUS 2 towards a supernatural Halloween adventure. A copy of the larger game is not required. The framing allows the story to step away from the main continuity, using a recognisable hero as the subject of a deliberately unreliable performance. The city becomes a place to explore through abilities that belong to Zeke's unlikely account.

cards.heading: Zeke tells a story with a darker bite
cards.text: inFAMOUS: Festival of Blood is Sucker Punch's standalone PlayStation 3 action game, first released in North America on 25 October 2011. Zeke recounts an exaggerated tale in which Cole MacGrath becomes a vampire, turning the familiar city and powers of inFAMOUS 2 towards a supernatural Halloween adventure. A copy of the larger game is not required. The framing allows the story to step away from the main continuity, using a recognisable hero as the subject of a deliberately unreliable performance. The city becomes a place to explore through abilities that belong to Zeke's unlikely account.

cards.heading: Move through the city as something else
cards.text: Vampiric powers change the way Cole crosses the city and deals with its inhabitants. Drinking blood restores health, removing the moral structure that shaped choices in the main games. The player is therefore encouraged to inhabit a more monstrous version of the character rather than carefully preserve a familiar heroic alignment. The shorter adventure concentrates on that variation, giving a known environment another atmosphere and another set of practical possibilities. Moving across rooftops and seeking the next objective becomes part of a supernatural story whose narrator has already given himself permission to embellish.

cards.heading: A compact experiment beside the main series
cards.text: The release also supported PlayStation Move and extended the user-created mission tools with a comic-scene feature. Its music combines contributions from Galactic, Jim Dooley, Brain and JD Mayer. Festival of Blood later joined the first two inFAMOUS games in the PlayStation 3 collection. As a standalone side story, it demonstrates what a familiar game world can support when the normal narrative rules are relaxed. The player recognises Cole and the city, but the telling changes what both can become, making the expansion a purposeful variation rather than another repetition of the main campaign.

main.title: Battlefield 3
main.summary: Battlefield 3 is a 2011 first-person shooter game developed by DICE and published by Electronic Arts.

cards.heading: Blackburn and Mayakovsky at war
cards.text: Battlefield 3 is a 2011 first-person shooter game developed by DICE and published by Electronic Arts. It is the twelfth installment in the Battlefield series and a sequel to Battlefield 2 (2005). The game was released on Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in October 2011. The campaign takes place in various locations and follows the stories of two characters, Henry Blackburn, a U.S. Marine and Dimitri Mayakovsky, a Spetsnaz GRU operative.

cards.heading: Frostbite and the September 2011 beta
cards.text: Development on the game began in 2009 after the release of Battlefield 1943. DICE employed an upgraded version of the Frostbite game engine to present realistic and engaging graphics. The public open beta ran from September 29 to October 10, 2011. Eligible Medal of Honor: Limited Edition or Tier 1 Edition players and qualifying Origin pre-orders received 48 hours of early access, starting on September 27.

cards.heading: Multiplayer acclaim and a successful launch
cards.text: Following its announcement, Battlefield 3 received much anticipation and hype. The game received mostly positive reviews from critics who praised its multiplayer and graphics, but criticized the campaign and cooperative modes. It sold 5 million copies in its first week of release, becoming one of the biggest launch titles of 2011. The game's sequel, Battlefield 4, was released in 2013.

main.title: Sonic Generations
main.subtitle: Two Sonics meet across twenty years
main.summary: Sonic Generations is a 2011 platform game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, Windows, and Nintendo 3DS.

cards.heading: Two Sonics meet across twenty years
cards.text: Sonic Generations is a 2011 platform game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, Windows, and Nintendo 3DS. Produced in commemoration of the 20th anniversary of the Sonic the Hedgehog series, the game follows Sonic and his sidekick Tails as they form an alliance with their past selves and travel through levels from previous Sonic games. It features two gameplay styles: "Classic", which plays from a side-scrolling perspective like that of the original Sega Genesis Sonic games, and "Modern", 3D levels similar to those in Sonic Unleashed (2008) and Sonic Colors (2010).

cards.heading: Classic and modern abilities
cards.text: Sonic Generations is a platform game in which players control two variants of Sonic the Hedgehog: "Classic" or "Modern". Classic Sonic's gameplay is restricted side-scrolling gameplay similar to the original Sonic the Hedgehog games released in the 1990s, and requires him to use moves such as the Spin Dash and the Spin Attack. Modern Sonic's gameplay follows the gameplay style of Sonic Unleashed (2008), and Sonic Colors (2010), featuring an amalgamation of third-person and side-scrolling perspectives and techniques such as boosting and homing attacks. Both Sonics collect rings as a form of health, and power-ups such as elemental shields, invincibility, speed shoes, skateboards, or Wisps. Players can also customize each Sonic's abilities, and purchase additional ones at a Skill Shop.

cards.heading: Older places are rebuilt for new play
cards.text: Sega used staff and public surveys to choose remembered stages, then rebuilt them rather than reuse their old assets. That created a translation problem: a location designed around three-dimensional movement needed a different route and rhythm in two dimensions. Even the classic Sonic controls required adjustment within the Hedgehog Engine, originally built for 3D play. A quicker Spin Dash helped unfamiliar players begin moving. The 3DS version followed its own selection of more recent handheld stages, adapting the anniversary's idea to different hardware.

main.title: Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception
main.subtitle: An adventure shaped by fire, water, air and sand
main.summary: Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception reached PlayStation 3 in North America on November 1, 2011. Naughty Dog built its adventure around unstable environments and the contrast between spectacle and isolation.

cards.heading: Nathan Drake heads into the desert
cards.text: Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception was released in North America for PlayStation 3 on November 1, 2011. Naughty Dog continued the cinematic adventure of Uncharted 2, taking Nathan Drake across several countries and into the Arabian desert. Its large action sequences depended on close collaboration between animation, programming, level design, sound and performance capture. Alongside that spectacle, the campaign made room for vulnerability: Drake could lose his bearings and struggle to keep moving, rather than always appear in control.

cards.heading: Four materials change the action
cards.text: Fire, water, air and sand gave the campaign four different kinds of physical situation. A burning building altered routes and timing; a tilting ship made floors and cover unstable; the airplane shifted the player's sense of space; and the desert removed familiar landmarks. These sequences demanded more than an impressive background. Animation, scripted events and level design had to work together while the player continued to move and respond. Alternating these environments also allowed the adventure to change pace between action and quieter stretches.

cards.heading: How the cargo plane was built
cards.text: Kurt Margenau recalled a sequence that began with chasing an aircraft along a runway, then boarding it and surviving its crash. The team used physical vehicle models to plan the action, wires during performance capture, and collaboration between animators, programmers and sound designers. A continuously scrolling desert made the aircraft appear to advance while it remained essentially stationary. Developing the sequence occupied much of the two-year production. A playable zero-gravity section was also tried, but did not reach the finished game.

cards.heading: A quieter journey through the sand
cards.text: After the plane, the pace slows as Drake crosses the desert with few landmarks. Lead designer Richard Lemarchand cited Lawrence of Arabia as a cinematic reference for the scale and disorientation of this sequence. Exhausted movement and hallucinations involving Sully convey Drake's vulnerability. Space, silence and repetition replace the aircraft's speed and noise. Keeping the player in control of that difficult walk makes fatigue and isolation part of the experience, rather than simply showing them in a cutscene.

cards.heading: Multiplayer and The Lab
cards.text: The multiplayer team also continued the experiments of Uncharted 2. In the tenth-anniversary retrospective, Evan Wells described a small team developing improved maps, new features, timed modes and experimental maps through The Lab. Multiplayer brought the series' movement, cover and vertical spaces into repeatable competitive matches. The Lab provided a way to try ideas and observe players' responses, making updates and experimentation an important part of the game's life after launch.

features.title: A scene is made between people
features.summary: Uncharted's performances depended on casting, animation, writing and collaboration.

cards.heading: Casting a relationship
cards.text: When describing Uncharted 2's cinematics, Amy Hennig starts with casting. Actors needed to suit a part and work convincingly with Nolan North, so auditions and callbacks tested relationships as well as individual performances. The production brought actors together on a sound stage and recorded their voices with their movement. Hennig wanted the hesitations, overlaps and responses that arise when people can actually react to one another. The scene's emotional detail therefore depended partly on how the work was organised before any finished digital character appeared.

cards.heading: The work after a performance
cards.text: Recording did not finish the scene. In the same production account, cinematic animation lead Josh Scherr explains that faces were animated by hand, using video of the actors as reference. Animators edited captured movement, fixed hands and feet, and adjusted gestures and contact between characters. Taylor Kurosaki helped turn camera coverage into an edited sequence. Their work complicates the idea that performance capture simply transfers acting into a game. The result passed through choices about timing, framing and expression, with different specialists making the performance readable.

cards.heading: Keeping a project coherent
cards.text: In a 2010 interview, Hennig describes creative direction as keeping a view of the entire project while colleagues worked on its parts. Her responsibilities included writing, working with actors and discussing game design with the game director. She also described earlier projects on which teammates supplied ideas or scene drafts that she helped make coherent. This account places authorship inside a production relationship. A recognisable voice can involve responsibility for revision and consistency, rather than requiring every useful idea to have begun with the same person.

cards.heading: Ideas change in company
cards.text: Hennig's explanation of inspiration likewise includes other people. Actors could reveal possibilities in a scene, while colleagues combined and challenged ideas until something emerged that neither would have produced alone. Films, television, books and other games also supplied material to consider. The important work was not just collecting references. It was deciding how those influences could live together within this game, with its characters and rules. The collaboration she describes gives a scene more than additional labour: it changes what the scene can become during development.

main.title: Super Mario 3D Land
main.subtitle: A bridge between 2D and 3D Mario
main.summary: Released in Japan on November 3, 2011, Super Mario 3D Land brought the clear goals of side-scrolling Mario into three-dimensional courses on Nintendo 3DS.

cards.heading: Mario returns to the flagpole
cards.text: Super Mario 3D Land was released in Japan for Nintendo 3DS on November 3, 2011. Its team wanted to bridge the gap between the linear two-dimensional games and the more open exploration of three-dimensional Mario. The end-of-level flagpole returned as a clear destination, while Star Medals gave players reasons to search beyond the main route. The game also used the handheld's stereoscopic display, but its environments had to remain understandable with the 3D effect switched off.

cards.heading: A clear route with room to explore
cards.text: The developers described the game as a missing link between 2D and 3D Mario. Instead of searching an open area for a Star, players usually followed a route to a flagpole. Arrows, fences and camera angles helped show where to go, sometimes revealing the goal in the distance. Exploration remained important: Star Medals encouraged players to investigate other parts of a course. Reaching the flagpole and finding everything therefore offered different levels of challenge within the same space.

cards.heading: Depth, cameras and shadows
cards.text: The developers adjusted the camera and the strength of stereoscopy, and reduced visual density to make the game clearer and less tiring to view. Shadows supplied another useful cue: a shadow directly below a floating coin or block showed its position, even with the 3D slider off. The stereoscopic effect added information about jumps and heights without becoming the only way to read them. Tanooki Mario could also fall more slowly, helping players judge and correct their jumps.

cards.heading: Help after five failed attempts
cards.text: The Invincibility Leaf appeared after Mario was defeated five times. Takashi Tezuka supported this aid because it protected players from damage without completing the course for them: they still had to move, jump and reach the goal. The original plan required eight defeats, but the threshold was reduced to five. Players could finish a difficult section with help and return later to attempt it unaided. Assistance became part of Mario's familiar objects and rules, rather than removing the need to play.

main.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3
main.subtitle: The campaign continues the global conflict
main.summary: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 is a 2011 first-person shooter game developed by Infinity Ward and Sledgehammer Games and published by Activision.

cards.heading: The campaign continues the global conflict
cards.text: Infinity Ward and Sledgehammer Games developed Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3, published by Activision in 2011. The campaign begins immediately after Modern Warfare 2, following Captain Price, Soap MacTavish and new playable character Yuri as Task Force 141 hunts Vladimir Makarov. Delta Force and SAS operations form other perspectives on a widening conflict. Multiplayer adds modes and killstreak choices to the established progression.

cards.heading: Objectives guide the campaign
cards.text: The campaign shifts between playable characters across three acts. Objectives include reaching a position, holding against an attack, directing remote weapons or planting explosives. Companions fight alongside the player while health recovers after a period without damage. A scene depicting an attack on civilians can be skipped.

cards.heading: Survival adds escalating cooperative waves
cards.text: Survival sends one or two players against increasingly difficult enemy waves on multiplayer maps. Kills and assists earn cash for weapons, ammunition, upgrades and support, while experience opens further options. Special Ops also returns with a separate collection of short challenge missions.

main.title: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
main.subtitle: A world to explore beyond the main quest
main.summary: Bethesda Game Studios released Skyrim on November 11, 2011 for PC, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in North America and Europe. Its open world combined exploration, skill-based progression, dragons and a lasting modding community.

cards.heading: Skyrim opens on 11/11/11
cards.text: Bethesda Game Studios released The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim on November 11, 2011 for PC, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in North America and Europe. Its open world scattered quests, ruins and detours across a Nordic landscape of mountains, mist, wood and stone. Players could develop their abilities through use instead of choosing a fixed class at the beginning. Dragons and the powers called Shouts connected that freedom to the story of the Dragonborn. Mods and later editions helped extend the game's life far beyond its original launch.

cards.heading: Mountains and landmarks guide exploration
cards.text: The Throat of the World dominates the horizon, while cities, forts and ruins provide recognizable landmarks. Seeing a distant destination does not always reveal an easy path: mountains, changes in height and winding roads can demand a detour. The compass helps locate points of interest, but observation remains useful. The landscape repeatedly offers reasons to leave a chosen objective and investigate something else, making exploration a central part of the adventure.

cards.heading: Skills grow through use
cards.text: Character development follows what the player does. Using one-handed weapons, forging equipment, picking locks, casting spells or moving stealthily improves different skills. On leveling up, perks allow further specialization. Without a fixed starting class, players can change habits and develop a character through experience. Exploration and progression reinforce one another: discovering a mine, forging a weapon and then using it can become parts of the same journey.

cards.heading: Dragon souls and Shouts
cards.text: Dragons link combat with exploration and progression. The Dragonborn learns words from Word Walls and uses absorbed dragon souls to unlock their power. Shouts combine words into abilities, encouraging the search for tombs, mountains and ruins. A dragon can also interrupt travel in the open world and turn a village or valley into a battlefield. The ancient language is therefore more than story background: its words become powers with different effects and cooldowns.

cards.heading: Stories inside the ruins
cards.text: Nordic tombs, forts, caves and Dwemer complexes suggest different histories through architecture, materials, traps, bodies and objects. Journals and notes add information, but the arrangement of a room can also suggest what happened there. Shortcuts near entrances can reduce the return journey, while larger chambers prepare encounters or rewards. Exploring a ruin means reading these clues as well as fighting enemies and searching for treasure.

cards.heading: Building the look of the North
cards.text: Wood, iron, fur, stone and Nordic motifs give Skyrim a consistent visual identity. Concept artists and modelers translated designs for armor, creatures and buildings into objects that had to belong to the same world. Cities and factions could look different without losing that shared vocabulary. Strong silhouettes and recognizable materials were important within the technical limits of the original platforms. The result remained identifiable across later editions of the game.

cards.heading: A long life through mods
cards.text: On PC, the Creation Kit allowed the community to change quests, locations, rules, interfaces, objects and characters. Players created fixes, transformations and substantial new works. Bethesda later supported mods on console editions too, with restrictions that varied by platform. Anniversary celebrations acknowledged the community's role in keeping Skyrim alive. Its longevity came not only from official rereleases, but also from authors who could keep correcting, expanding and reinterpreting the same world.

features.title: Making pieces fit
features.summary: Artists build systems that other people can use.

cards.heading: An ugly kit starts work
cards.text: Skyrim's rooms depended on a conversation between level designers and the artists making their architectural pieces. Joel Burgess and Nate Purkeypile described beginning with a functional kit before polishing its appearance. Designers could test spaces while artists continued developing the parts, rather than waiting for a finished collection of beautiful objects. An unattractive prototype could already answer whether pieces worked together and supported movement. Making that early version usable protected time for both kinds of work, keeping the level's needs involved as its surfaces became richer.

cards.heading: Names and pivots matter
cards.text: A kit also needed names that others could understand. Burgess and Purkeypile recalled obscure abbreviations making an earlier collection harder to use, and explained why shared naming conventions helped designers find pieces. The position around which an object rotated mattered as much. Changing that pivot after hundreds of copies had been placed could leave a large repair job. These decisions sat behind the visible scenery, yet they shaped what colleagues could build efficiently. Maintaining a world included maintaining the small agreements that held its parts together.

cards.heading: Try the wall twice
cards.text: Environment artist Thiago Klafke put a different project through a similar practical test. His Zest Foundation tutorial urged makers to export pieces early and assemble them inside the engine. A wall that looked good alone might look poor when repeated, and neighbouring parts could expose gaps that a modelling view concealed. Testing the set changed the question from whether one object was attractive to whether it belonged in a working environment. The repeated wall became a tool for judging the original piece, not merely its final destination.

cards.heading: More from the same surfaces
cards.text: Klafke's texture planning sought variety from a small collection of surfaces. Wall textures, trims and floors could serve different shapes, while vertex colours helped vary their appearance. A trim could become part of another architectural detail instead of demanding a wholly new image. The tutorial connects that economy to experimentation: artists move between constructing a piece, applying a surface and seeing the result in the engine. Reuse still needs judgement about seams, proportions and repetition. The collection becomes useful through how its parts are arranged and adapted.

main.title: Saints Row: The Third
main.summary: Saints Row: The Third is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Volition and published by THQ.

cards.heading: The original release and later editions
cards.text: Volition developed Saints Row: The Third, published by THQ in November 2011 for Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It moves the series from Stilwater to Steelport, where the Saints must rebuild their strength. Later ports and a remastered edition brought the adventure to additional platforms.

cards.heading: The Saints take on Steelport
cards.text: The game is set in the fictional city of Steelport and continues the story of the 3rd Street Saints, once again placing players in the role of the gang's leader, who is fully customizable. Years after the events of Saints Row 2, the Saints have grown from their humble origins as a street gang into a large media and consumer empire with their own brand, while many of the gang's members have become celebrities and pop culture icons. After being stranded in Steelport, which is firmly ruled by an international crime organization known as the Syndicate, the Saints must rebuild their forces once more to take over the city and defeat the Syndicate, as well as S.T.A.G., a violent paramilitary contracted with restoring order to Steelport.

cards.heading: A new team finds a coherent tone
cards.text: Development of Saints Row: The Third began in late 2008, shortly after the release of Saints Row 2. There was high staff turnover from the previous Saints Row team, with only one-fifth of the final 100-person staff having worked on a previous title in the series. They aimed to improve on the series by giving the game a coherent tone, and found it in films such as Hot Fuzz and the game's signature sex toy bat.

cards.heading: Reception, expansions and Saints Row IV
cards.text: The game received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its general zaniness and customization options. Criticism was aimed at the new setting, which many critics felt was flat and underdeveloped compared to the previous games' Stilwater, and the lackluster humor. On the contrary, others thought the game perfected the Saints Row formula. It was a nominee for Best Narrative at the 2012 Game Developers Conference, an IGN Editor's Choice, and a recipient of perfect scores from GamesRadar and G4. A complete edition including the three downloadable content packs was released in 2012, and its planned Enter the Dominatrix expansion became the game's sequel, Saints Row IV, released in 2013.

main.title: Rayman Origins
main.subtitle: Rayman returns to the platform game
main.summary: Rayman Origins is a 2011 platform game developed and published by Ubisoft.

cards.heading: Rayman returns to the platform game
cards.text: Rayman Origins is a 2011 platform game developed and published by Ubisoft. It is the fourth main installment in the Rayman series and the first main installment following Rayman 3: Hoodlum Havoc (2003). The game was released for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Wii platforms worldwide, with PlayStation Vita, Nintendo 3DS, and Microsoft Windows versions being released the following year. The OS X version of the game was released on December 12, 2013, by Feral Interactive. The story follows Rayman, his friend Globox, and two Teensies as they fight Darktoons and other evil creatures that have infected the Glade of Dreams after they unleashed said evil by complete accident.

cards.heading: Four players share the screen
cards.text: Rayman Origins is a side-scrolling platformer, the same style as the original Rayman game. Rayman Origins is playable with up to four local players who may drop in or out at any time. Players can choose to control either Rayman, Globox or two Teensies, with additional costumes available as the game progresses.

cards.heading: UbiArt keeps the drawing in motion
cards.text: UbiArt Framework brings drawn characters and scenery into motion by deforming and animating two-dimensional artwork. The tools were designed to let artists and designers work directly with that material. Ubisoft supported their development with a French arts grant. The engine continued into Rayman Legends, which added dynamic lighting and three-dimensional elements.

main.title: Assassin's Creed Revelations
main.subtitle: Ezio's final chapter
main.summary: Assassin's Creed: Revelations is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft.

cards.heading: Ezio's final chapter
cards.text: Assassin's Creed: Revelations is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft. It is the fourth major installment of the Assassin's Creed series, and a direct sequel to 2010's Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood, concluding the "Ezio Trilogy". The game was released on PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Microsoft Windows in November and December 2011. A remastered version of Revelations, along with Assassin's Creed II and Brotherhood, was released as part of The Ezio Collection compilation for the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One on November 15, 2016, and for the Nintendo Switch on February 17, 2022.

cards.heading: The Hookblade changes traversal and combat
cards.text: Ezio and Alta?r retain the series' combination of combat, stealth and climbing, while Desmond supplies another perspective. Ezio's new Hookblade extends his reach when climbing, crosses larger gaps and uses ziplines. It also adds combat moves for pulling enemies into an attack.

cards.heading: Bomb crafting adds tactical choices
cards.text: Another new aspect of the game is bomb crafting. Introduced early on in the story, this mechanic allows Ezio to experiment with different shells and ingredients to create bombs with various effects, such as smoke to distract guards or lethal explosions that can take out large groups of enemies. There are around 15 different bomb variations in the game, although only three can be equipped at any given time.
